title: Protein supplementation and resistance-training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength: a systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression (Morton et al. 2018)
content: Morton RW et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine 2018 — Meta-analysis of 49 studies (1863 participants) found protein supplementation significantly increased resistance-training-induced gains in fat-free mass and strength versus training alone. Meta-regression showed the benefit of additional protein plateaus around ~1.6 g/kg/day total daily protein intake; intakes beyond that showed no further average benefit for muscle mass in the pooled data, though individual response varies.

title: Protein supplementation and resistance-training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength: a systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression (Morton et al. 2018)
content: Morton et al. 2018 — Product implication: 1.6 g/kg/day is a reasonable practical target/starting point for muscle-gain-focused protein intake in most resistance-trained individuals, consistent with (and inside) the ISSN 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day range — not a hard ceiling, and higher intakes are not shown harmful in healthy adults, but the marginal benefit for hypertrophy specifically diminishes above this level.
